utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you very well. PRESIDING OFFICER: Good. Fine. Mr. Withopf, I think you're continuing with your questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, good morning. Mr. Karic, there are two documents I wish to discuss with you today, and you will certainly be able to assist us with the interpretation of such documents. Such documents have been made available to the court deputy in Sarajevo yesterday afternoon. The documents have also been made available in both B/C/S and English language to Defence counsel, and it's my understanding that they are also available to the Presiding Officer. The Prosecution tenders both documents into evidence, named as PVK 1 and PVK 2. Mr. Karic -- PRESIDING OFFICER: Just before you carry on, would you like us to deal with the admission of those now or at the end of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Right now. PRESIDING OFFICER: Right now? Mr. Hodzic, would you have any objection to the -- I gather you've been provided with the two documents. Do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] PRESIDING OFFICER: For the record, the Defence counsel responded that he had no objection. Thank you. So Madam Registrar will give them a number for the purposes of this deposition.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first document will be numbered VK 1, and second attached document, VK 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, the two documents, the first one is the order of the accused Sefer Halilovic of 2nd September, 1993, and the second document is the urgent request for departure of units from the 1st Corps, also dated the 2nd of September, 1993. I understand these documents are available to you, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to read such documents?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Let's start with the first document, Mr. Karic. That's the order of the 2nd September, 1993. At the time, and in your capacity, Mr. Karic, of member of the group of high-ranking officers in Jablanica, did you get to know about this order?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The time you knew about it, have you been involved in discussing this order or even in the drafting of this order?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember being involved in its compilation. I was involved in compiling most of these orders, because there were several orders, a number of orders and communiques that we compiled over those few days. But I am familiar with the substance of the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The substance of this order touches on issues we already addressed yesterday. Yesterday you informed us, Mr. Karic, that it was Rasim Delic, commander of the Supreme Command staff of the ABiH, and the commander of the 1st Corps in Sarajevo, Karavelic, who ordered the 9th and the 10th Brigades to go to Jablanica. Why was there a need for the accused Sefer Halilovic to again order exactly the very same?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed this matter yesterday. There were certain obstructions. Caco, the commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade, caused certain obstructions. Sefer spoke to him subsequently. I think that was on the 5th, in the evening, or on the 6th of September. When Rasim Delic arrived in Jablanica, to our command post in Donja Jablanica, in the command of Zulfikar Alispago, the need was felt. He there signed all the documents relating to the operation, and we returned to Konjic in the evening hours and we spent the night there. He insisted on Sefer using his influence to do everything by going to Sarajevo to ensure that these units would obey the orders, and this was done. On the 5th, Sefer headed in the direction of Sarajevo, and he used his influence to ensure that those units departed, left. But this was with the authorisation of the commander of the Main Staff, Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Right. With the authorisation of the commander of the Main Staff, Rasim Delic. But wasn't Rasim Delic's order sufficient? Why was there a need that Sefer Halilovic ordered the 9th and 10th Brigades to go to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I spoke about this in detail. The military organisation at the time was such as it was. It wasn't very mature. It was necessary to persist and to exercise one's authority in order to provide remedies for certain issues, whereas in normal armies, in normal situations, such remedies would not be appropriate. In our case, we had to do this, and this is not the only case. Throughout the war. In addition to the orders issued by certain men, it was necessary to intervene. It was necessary to carry out similar actions, because the state of the military organisation, the state of the discipline, was very far from what one would have expected in similar situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May I interrupt you at this point?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- especially in armies, which have a certain tradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May I interrupt you at this point, Mr. Karic. In what capacity did Sefer Halilovic issue this particular order?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All he did was to insist that the order of the command of the Main Staff, Rasim Delic, should be obeyed. The order of the most senior officer in the army of the BH at the time. And through his influence, as the chief of staff in the Supreme Command, in the Main Staff, by arriving at Hrasnica and talking to Caco, he ensured that this order was finally obeyed and that those units headed towards Jablanica. And I'd like to point out yet again that Rasim Delic, in the ARK, in Konjic, where we spent the night together, agreed and suggested to Sefer that he go to Sarajevo and that he accelerate the departure of the units, because it was obvious that there were obstructions, that Caco, in particular, was making it difficult for this order to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Moving on, Mr. Karic, to item 2 of this order, item 2 reads: "If you consider that such redeployment endangers the defence of Sarajevo, I am prepared to bear full responsibility." Can you please assist us in the interpretation of this portion of the order?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As throughout the entire period, in the case of Vahid Karavelic, as the commander of the 1st Corps, the person who was most responsible for the defence of the town, as he was afraid that by separating units for the defence of Sarajevo, he would be putting the defence of Sarajevo at risk, given this fear, Sefer thought that if he thought that this endangered the defence of Sarajevo, he would bear the responsibility personally, and he wanted to point out once again that he was aware of the fact that the defence of Sarajevo would not be put at risk by taking such action and that if it were put at risk, he would take the blame, not Karavelic. But order should be obeyed and the units sent as ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In terms of military hierarchy, Mr. Karic, wouldn't it have been Rasim Delic who should have ordered this or should have made such a remark to the command of the 1st Corps? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For all of us, and before heading to the command in the Vranica building, Rasim Delic issued clear orders to all those who were present, and similarly to Vahid Karavelic. So there was nothing that was ambiguous. But matters became complicated for the reasons that I have already mentioned. The military organisation and individual commanders within our military organisation was not as mature as it should have been, and the military relationships, military subordination was not as it should have been. And this demonstrated a lack of preparedness, and there was a storm which delayed everything. And after they got to Hrasnica, there was another delay of 24 hours. And whether they would leave was in question. Rasim Delic headed towards Zenica and visited us, but it wasn't necessary for him to return. He told Sefer and ordered Sefer that it would be good for him to go to Sarajevo and to use his personal authority to accelerate everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, what was the accused's, Sefer Halilovic's role during Operation NERETVA-93?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we spoke about this matter yesterday. He was the key person from the inspection team, from the entire group involved in that task. But in terms of office, he was the chief of the Main Staff of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: As part of this team you were just mentioning, did he have any command functions?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the order that we received from Rasim Delic for the inspection team to go into the field and carry out inspections, the function of command was taken away from Sefer and the entire team, and this was felt in the order itself. We were not in a position to order anything to anyone, given that we knew that this team had an inspection function. Its function was to control, to inspect. And people accepted us in the subordinate brigades that we were in. They respected us, first of all as fighters, as people who were experienced and who held the positions that we held.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they weren't in a position, nor did they have to carry out any of our orders. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, may I interrupt you at this point? Isn't it a little bit contradictional to what you are saying that Sefer Halilovic issued an order on the 2nd of September, during Operation NERETVA-93, and you are saying now he didn't have any power to do so? Can you please assist us in clarifying this issue.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to tell you that the units and commands respected us as people from the Supreme Command, but on the basis of the order that we received from Sarajevo, we did not have the authority to command and take command decisions in those units. So from the very beginning, we were not a command that had all the prerogatives of a command and the ability to issue orders. Everything was based on implementing Rasim Delic's order, according to which we were part of the inspection team. I think I have been clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, have you been interviewed by OTP investigators in the course of last year?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you have a recollection of this interview?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a few days.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The beginning of the sentence was missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, do you have a recollection of this interview?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I remember the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, in the course of this interview, you were mentioning that there was a temporary command post, and you were making reference to the same group of people we are talking about today. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had to be accommodated somewhere, and we were accommodated in the office of the director of an Elektroprivreda company, the Jablanica station. But that wasn't a forward command post or a temporary command post in the traditional sense of the term. We had to establish or maintain contact with people from some position. We had to be accommodated somewhere, although this was temporary. And during the preparations that took several days, we spent most of the time there, and the remainder of the time in the units and their commands, and this was not a temporary command post in the traditional sense, with its prerogatives, with its communication centre, with all its organs and the commands, it's not as if reports were submitted to them daily and it's not as if they issued dozens of orders every day, as is the case when commands have such authority. But we were in a position to find accommodation and to work from there. We used the communication system of another brigade. We didn't have our own. And it was far from being a temporary command post or a forward command post, because we didn't have the organs and we weren't in the position to issue orders and to form a forward command post or a temporary command post. But our role was to coordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, you are --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To coordinate the cooperation between the -- please, may I finish what I have to say. It's very important. If we don't manage to clarify these matters. It's very important. From the outset, we were not in such a position to have temporary command post there and to have the prerogative of issuing orders. The inspection team did not have the right to order anything. They would have to submit a report to Rasim Delic and then Rasim Delic, as the senior officer in the Main Staff, would have to issue an order, if it was necessary to replace someone or to use a certain unit, et cetera. All the action we took was in accordance with the decisions taken by Rasim Delic and the orders that we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, you are a person of a pretty high military rank and you are certainly not using military terms in an ambiguous way. In your statement given to the OTP investigators, you several times spoke about a temporary command post. You several times, Mr. Karic, made reference to the accused's role as a commander, and you several times mentioned and you several times underlined that he has been the person in command. Can you clarify why you are today telling us something that appears to be very different from your previous statement?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was convinced that there was no difference, if you listen to me carefully. Sefer, as the chief of staff of the BH army, at the beginning of September 1993 in the Jablanica area, while preparing the NERETVA-93 operation, had credibility as the chief of staff of our army, and people respected him as such. As far as the temporary command post is concerned, we can't call it anything else, because we were accommodated in a building, in a facility in Jablanica, where we could carry out the work as a team, the work that we had been assigned in the order. Perhaps because of a lack of some other official term for such a situation, perhaps because of this lack, I called it a temporary command post. But according to military theory, military terminology, if a temporary command post, if we have a temporary command post, it has all the prerogatives, all the communication system, but it's in a position to carry out all tasks from that position. It can issue orders, it can receive reports, et cetera. And this is not something that we could do from that position. So I don't see any significant difference here, whether it's a temporary or stationary. We spent a few days there working and establishing contact with commands which were involved in the NERETVA-93 operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, wouldn't you agree that there's a very clear military terminology in distinguishing what is called a forward command post, a temporary command post, and a team with the functions you are referring to, namely, an inspection team? And you, as a commander of a very high rank at the time, certainly knew about this difference?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to tell you that I was aware of this then, as I am now. There is a significant difference according to military terminology, a difference between a temporary and a forward command post. A command got tasks and authority to carry out a certain task, technical equipment, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. logistics, a certain number of posts were assigned, et cetera. The four of us didn't have the -- weren't in a position to issue orders. We didn't have the strength. There weren't enough of us to constitute a temporary or forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: But don't you agree, Mr. Karic, that Mr. Sefer Halilovic, in the course of the Operation NERETVA-93, issued orders, for example, the order of 2nd September we were talking about previously?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He issued orders. That's absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units carried out those orders. But that was all within the framework of orders issued by the commander of the chief staff with regard to carrying out the NERETVA-93 operation. There was nothing outside the framework of such orders or outside the scope of the authority that Rasim Delic had with regard to the NERETVA-93 operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, I have to ask you this question: Have you, between the statement you've given to OTP investigators in December last year and your testimony today, have you been contacted by anybody who talked to you about your today's testimony?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did anybody contact me?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In the sense that somebody talked to you about your role in Operation NERETVA-93, the role of the accused, Mr. Sefer Halilovic in Operation NERETVA-93, and your statement you've given previously to the OTP investigators.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no, no. No one. And indeed, there are no grounds for putting such a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The reason why I'm putting to you such a question is the obvious discrepancy between your statement you've given to us in December 2002 and your yesterday's and today's testimony. Did you on your own talk to somebody about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. When I say no, it's no. There was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Featherstone, the Prosecution tenders the previous statement, the statement given to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor in December 2002 into evidence, please. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Mr. Hodzic, do you have any objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have an objection, because the statement that this witness is making now differs from the previous one he made. However, in terms of terminology, in terms of the position Mr. Karic held and his high rank, this -- there is a complete coincidence in terms of terminology in respect of what he said today. We have objections in terms of the translation of documents that were provided by the OTP. There are many errors in translation and in terminology in the statements taken by witnesses. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. As you're aware, I am not empowered to rule on any objection. I simply refer it to the Trial Chamber for a decision. I don't know, Mr. Withopf, if there's anything short you would like to respond to Mr. Hodzic. This is your opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: At least in respect to the issue of translation, Defence counsel didn't raise any issue in translation of the concrete statement. Therefore, I don't think this is any valid concern he raised in that respect. Otherwise, the witness has been interviewed as a suspect, according to the Rules, and there is no reason to not tender the transcript of the previous statement into evidence. PRESIDING OFFICER: Can I just clarify for the record as well,

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you know when this statement was disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes. I know that. If you give me a second, I can give a very detailed answer to this question. PRESIDING OFFICER: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The respective motion of the Prosecution to take a deposition of the witness Karic was filed on 14th of March this year, together with a motion, there has been the full transcript of the interview of the witness in English language been disclosed, and Defence got the full transcript of the B/C/S translation on 23rd of May this year. There was sufficient time for the Defence to prepare. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. And simply so that the Trial Chamber have everything before them, they would need to determine this matter, Mr. Hodzic, is there anything you would like to add, simply as to the question of admission of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Madam Presiding Officer. I would just like to say that the witnesses, including witness Karic signed the statements that were presented to them in the English language, after the translation was made. They never saw for themselves what they wrote and what they signed. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. That full debate will of course be passed to the Trial Chamber for consideration. Mr. Withopf, do you have more questions relating to the documents? Because I have one small point that I would like clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I have one or two questions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sorry. I have one or two questions in relation to the second document. PRESIDING OFFICER: Fine. Then I'll put my question at the end. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The second document, Mr. Karic, the second order, it has in its fourth line the initials SHVK. Does VK stand for Vehbija Karic?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does this mean, Mr. Karic, that you have been involved in drafting the order?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What's the background for this order?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this situation when one had to wait and see, because the operation was already running late because the units had not come, and the reports of the subordinate units, especially of the 4th Corps, was alarming, that an attack was being expected any moment against these units and on the left bank of the Neretva River. That is to say, the 4th Corps and the Bosniak part of Mostar. That is why we made an attempt in this way as well to speed up the departure of our units from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And I again ask you the question, Mr. Karic: Why did not Rasim Delic and/or Vahid Karavelic in his function, as the command of the 1st Corps, request the departure of the troops?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, until the present day, I believe that they did ask for that. Vahid Karavelic, commander of the 1st Corps, particularly insisted on having this order honoured and carried out. I assume that Rasim Delic, after having issued this order, namely, that these units should leave, was not totally uninterested in this respect. He wanted them to leave, indeed. Now, whether he intervened, and in which way, whether he did this verbally or in some other way, that is something I don't know. But what I do know for sure is that he did issue this order in the presence of all the heads of department -- all the members of the General Staff, at the proposal of Vahid Karavelic, he accepted that, and that is why we were expecting these units to come. And at that moment, nobody wanted to obstruct this, to have this order just left dangling without the units actually leaving town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: But wouldn't you agree, Mr. Karic, that it is a very unusual situation that you have an order by the head of the army, that you have an order by the 1st Corps commander, and there's still a need for the accused, Sefer Halilovic, to order the 1st Corps commander to send troops?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a normal situation, it would only be normal to put such a question. However, in the situation that we lived in and in terms of the military organisation that existed in September 1993 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we were not in a position to do so. Whatever we did, we did in order to succeed in carrying out military activity as planned and to have these orders carried out. But obviously, they were being obstructed, which was manifested through everything that we are discussing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Karic. I have only one further issue to discuss, but I think it will take me some 20 minutes, and the Presiding Officer has made an announcement that she wishes to address something else. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Perhaps you could clarify with the witness, Mr. Withopf: The two documents, each one bears a stamp from the date on which it was received at the Supreme Command, and I note that on the second document, that date is the 2nd of September, 1993. It's roughly in the middle of the page of the English translation. So that's contemporaneous with the date of the document. On the first document, it's dated the 1st of March, 1994. Now, it may well be that this is something beyond the knowledge of this witness, but we should just clarify that, if it is something that he has any knowledge about or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Featherstone. I assume it's beyond the knowledge of the witness; however, we will ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, you understood what the Presiding Officer has addressed? Mr. Karic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this document. As I mentioned a short while ago. But as for this particular coincidence, the date from 1994, et cetera, I'm surprised by that, because in terms of the date when we sent it and in terms of when it was received, this is the shorter order of the 3rd of September, 1993. It was sent to the 4th and 1st Corps on the 3rd of September. And the other order of the 2nd of September was also sent on the 2nd of September, 1993, to Commander Rasim -- or rather, the commander of the 1st Corps, the commander of the Main Staff of the Supreme Command received a copy, as well as the commander of the 6th Corps. In terms of any delays, administrative delays, I'm not aware of any. I proceed from the assumption that they received them on the same day when they were sent. PRESIDING OFFICER: That's fine for my purposes. Thank you, Mr. Karic and Mr. Withopf. Actually, while we're at a short break in the proceedings, Madam Registrar has reminded me that the statement of Mr. Karic should of course be marked for identification for the record. Does it require a number, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be numbered -- marked for identification, MFI Prosecution 2. We would need to have copies for the Chamber and Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The copies are available. Four copies are available and the fifth copy will be provided after the break. There's one further issue the Prosecution wishes to address with the witness. It will take us some 20 to 30 minutes. I don't know whether it would be wise to have the break right now or later on. PRESIDING OFFICER: Let's see how the witness feels. Mr. Karic, you heard that. Mr. Withopf would like to question you for about another half an hour or so. Would you like that we take the 15-minute break now and resume at half past 10.00? I don't think it would be good to interrupt part way through. I think we either break now or we allow Mr. Withopf to go all the way through and take a later break. Which would be your preference, Mr. Karic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would rather that we continue our work and then we'll take a rest after that. PRESIDING OFFICER: Fine. We'll do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Karic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I'm moving on to a different issue, Mr. Karic. That's the knowledge of the accused, Mr. Sefer Halilovic, about the crime in Grabovica. To your knowledge, when did the accused, Mr. Sefer Halilovic, get to know about the murders in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found out - Zicro Suljevic, Rifat Bilajac and I - in Jablanica on the 8th of September, around 11.00 in the morning, from Namik Dzankovic, the security officer, that a crime had been committed. In the first version, they said that 19 elderly, innocent Croats were killed and thrown into the Neretva River. Later on, the number was actually increased, as you know. And Sefer at that moment was not in Jablanica. He came the next day, or rather, the 9th, when we, that is to say, we and Djankovic informed him in detail about the crime that had been committed on the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In terms of the dates, Mr. Karic, there appears to be some confusion about the day, the 8th or the 9th of September. For clarification, when you, together with others, informed Mr. Sefer Halilovic, was it the day, the immediate day after the killings?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The day after the actual killings. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And at what time, to your recollection, has Mr. Halilovic been informed about the killings?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the morning, tentatively, in the morning hours, because that's when he returned to Jablanica from the field. Now, whether it was 10.00 or 11.00 a.m. -- well, anyway, it was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were saying, Mr. Karic, that Mr. Halilovic has been informed in detail. What actually has he been informed about?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was told that a crime had been committed in Grabovica, that it had been perpetrated by the members of the 9th and 10th Brigades. That's the information that we had then, on the basis of the briefing we received from Dzankovic, who in turn had received this information from the municipal Territorial Defence staff and the MUP, from Prozor, or rather, from Jablanica. And also he had contact himself with the units. These -- this particular information was not nearly detailed enough yet, either in terms of the number of victims or in terms of the actual kind of massacre that was carried out. But at that time, we knew about 19 victims. Later on, it was established that there were 31 victims, but this was later, much later. At first, we just knew that they were killed and thrown into the Neretva River. How they were killed, whether this was done by firearms or by knives, we had no idea, but Sefer and we issued orders to Dzankovic in terms of what he was supposed to do further on, to ask for reinforcement from the security administration so that detailed investigation could be carried out, also that the General Staff should receive a report, and also to cooperate with the security organs of the 44th Brigade and with the MUP and to continue collecting facts about the crime and its perpetrators. That is what Sefer ordered in detail, also in our presence, on the next day, when he was informed about all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, where has Mr. Halilovic been informed about the crime? Mr. Karic?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was at that place where we were staying, and that is Elektroprivreda, in Jablanica, in those offices of Elektroprivreda where we were staying. That's where he was made aware of this as soon as he came. I think that this was on the 9th of September, in the morning. In the morning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How far away is Jablanica from Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately four to five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, did Mr. Sefer Halilovic make any attempt, as the highest-ranking person in the area, to visit the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your knowledge --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And had he done this, I don't know what he would have seen, because the Neretva took the bodies away, so nothing was known. Perhaps his presence would have made the situation even more difficult, the investigation even more difficult, because the area had already been sealed off and the security organs of the 44th Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, may I interrupt you, please. To your knowledge, the question was: To your knowledge, did Mr. Halilovic visit the crime scene? The answer can only be yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Karic. The Prosecution finished its examination-in-chief. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you, Mr. Withopf, and compliments on your timeliness. Mr. Hodzic, will you be ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took a request in writing, and I'm not prepared to cross-examine because it was not sufficient to simply read the interview of Mr. Karic and then to cross-examine. What was necessary was to take a look at and analyse a series of other documents that are related to this case. So I abide by -- PRESIDING OFFICER: Sorry. I interrupted you. Please do finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's it. That's what I had to say. So for the time being, I'm not prepared to cross-examine. PRESIDING OFFICER: Right. In that case, I would actually -- there is something I would like to state to both the counsel. But we'll release the witness temporarily, certainly. So, Mr. Karic, we'll take our break now. I wish to discuss a couple of matters with counsel. So if you would stay in the building, please, and we'll let you know after the break whether or not you'll be asked any more questions. So we'll speak to you again shortly, shall we say at a quarter to 11.00? That's a 20-minute break from now. And if the court deputy could stay in contact with us via the videolink as well. Thank you, Mr. Karic. You may go. No, sorry. We're not adjourned yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Right. Mr. Hodzic, I heard what you had to say then, of course, and as I stated yesterday, the Trial Chamber has your application for withdrawal. I would just like to remind you, though, that, as you know, the witness's health is very poor, and that was the basic reason that the deposition was ordered. You are here, and you've heard all the evidence that's been given by the witness yesterday and today, and I really would encourage you to consider taking this opportunity to examine this witness, as it probably won't arise again. Now, if you do not, then obviously the Trial Chamber will be aware of that and bear it in mind when they assess the evidence of this witness. Now, as we have time available, what I would like to suggest is that perhaps we could adjourn until tomorrow, which would allow you some more time to prepare, some time to maybe contact your client and seek instructions from him about this, and perhaps you would be in a position to proceed tomorrow. What do you think about that course of action, that we adjourn until tomorrow and you then come back and advise whether or not you would be able to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your understanding. I accept your proposal, namely, that we adjourn today and that tomorrow I state my definite views on the matter. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you very much. Mr. Withopf, is there anything you would like to state at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Not for the moment. It depends on the final definite views of Defence counsel tomorrow. PRESIDING OFFICER: Of course. Now, I assume that Sarajevo can hear us. Can anyone confirm that to me?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I can hear you. PRESIDING OFFICER: Right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I can hear you. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Good morning, Evelyn. Perhaps you can inform the witness, then, that he won't be needed again today but if he can return at 9.30 tomorrow morning we'll know then exactly how -- whether we're proceeding tomorrow or whether that's finished. Okay. If you could inform him that. And in that case, then, we're adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 10th day of July 2003, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.29 a.m.,
